q: What is the most important prognostic factor for melanoma survival?
A patient presents with a pearly, slow-growing papule with telangiectasias on the upper lip. Diagnosis?
A patient with a history of organ transplant presents with a non-healing, ulcerated nodule with a keratin plug on the lower lip. Biopsy shows keratin pearls. Diagnosis?
What is the first-line treatment for multiple actinic keratoses (AK)?
a: Topical 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or imiquimod. (Note: cryotherapy for isolated lesions).

q: The sudden appearance of multiple seborrheic keratoses (Leser-Trélat sign) is associated with what underlying condition?
A patient has sharply demarcated, erythematous plaques with silvery scales on extensor surfaces. What is the phenomenon where minor trauma causes new lesions?
A healthy 20-year-old presents with a "herald patch" followed by a diffuse "Christmas tree" pattern scaling rash on the trunk. Diagnosis?
A patient with Hepatitis C presents with pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with fine white lines (Wickham striae) on the wrists. Diagnosis?
Targetoid lesions appearing abruptly on the extremities, often following a Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Diagnosis?
A severe mucocutaneous reaction characterized by epidermal sloughing involving <10% of total body surface area (TBSA), often triggered by medications like allopurinol or antiepileptics. Diagnosis?
A life-threatening mucocutaneous disease with extensive epidermal necrosis and sloughing involving >30% TBSA, with a positive Nikolsky sign. Diagnosis?
An elderly patient presents with intensely pruritic, tense subepidermal bullae. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane. Diagnosis?

A middle-aged patient presents with painful oral erosions and flaccid cutaneous bullae that easily rupture (positive Nikolsky sign). Immunofluorescence shows a net-like intraepidermal IgG pattern. Diagnosis?
A patient with Celiac disease presents with intensely pruritic papules and vesicles on the elbows and knees. Immunofluorescence shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae. Diagnosis?
a: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Tx: Dapsone and gluten-free diet).

q: A patient with Hepatitis C or hemochromatosis presents with painless blisters and skin fragility on the dorsum of the hands after sun exposure. Diagnosis?
a: Porphyria cutanea tarda (deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase).

q: What is the mechanism of action of isotretinoin (a derivative of vitamin A, C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>28</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) used for severe, nodulocystic acne vulgaris?
a: Decreases sebum production and normalizes epidermal desquamation. (Note: Highly teratogenic, requires two forms of contraception).

q: A patient presents with facial flushing, erythema, telangiectasias, and papulopustules on the nose and cheeks, worsened by alcohol and spicy foods. First-line topical treatment?
A chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by painful nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in the axillae and groin. Diagnosis?
A child presents with perioral honey-colored crusted lesions. What is the most common causative organism and first-line topical treatment?
a: Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Strep; Topical mupirocin.

q: A superficial bacterial skin infection causing a well-demarcated, raised, intensely erythematous plaque on the face or legs, most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus. Diagnosis?
A deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue infection presenting with ill-defined borders, erythema, swelling, and tenderness. Most common organisms?
A newborn presents with fever, generalized erythema, and large flaccid bullae that slough off with gentle pressure. Diagnosis?
a: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS, caused by exfoliative toxins).

q: A patient with rapidly spreading erythema, extreme pain out of proportion to exam findings, and crepitus on palpation. Next best step in management?
a: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement (Diagnosis: Necrotizing fasciitis).

q: Annular, erythematous plaques with a central clearing and a scaly, active border. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation shows branching septate hyphae. Diagnosis?
A teenager presents with hypopigmented macules on the upper back and chest that do not tan in the sun. KOH prep shows "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance. Diagnosis?
A child with a scaly patch of alopecia and broken hairs on the scalp. What is the treatment of choice?
a: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine (Topical antifungals are ineffective for Tinea capitis).

q: An obese patient with diabetes presents with an erythematous, highly pruritic rash with satellite lesions in the inframammary folds. Diagnosis?
Intensely pruritic, thread-like burrows in the interdigital web spaces and flexor surfaces of wrists, with itching worse at night. Treatment of choice?
a: Topical 5% permethrin cream applied from neck down, or oral ivermectin.

q: A school-aged child with intense scalp pruritus. Exam shows tiny, white, oval structures firmly attached to hair shafts. First-line treatment?
Firm, dome-shaped, flesh-colored, umbilicated papules. What is the causative agent and the condition to screen for in adults with extensive disease?
A pregnant woman presents with solitary or multiple cauliflower-like lesions on the vulva. Diagnosis and causative agent?
A sexually active patient presents with a diffuse, non-pruritic maculopapular rash that involves the palms and soles, accompanied by generalized lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis?
A patient hiking in the Northeast US develops an expanding, erythematous, target-like rash (Erythema migrans). What is the treatment of choice for pregnant women or children <8 years old?
A patient develops fever, headache, and a petechial rash that started on the wrists and ankles and spread centrally, after a tick bite in North Carolina. Treatment?
a: Doxycycline (always first-line, even in children) for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever.

q: An autoimmune condition characterized by the destruction of melanocytes, resulting in well-demarcated depigmented macules/patches, often associated with other autoimmune diseases. Diagnosis?
An infant presents with diffuse hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes. What enzyme is deficient?
a: Tyrosinase (Oculocutaneous albinism, inability to synthesize melanin from tyrosine).

q: Acquired hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas on the face, commonly seen in pregnancy or with oral contraceptive use. Diagnosis?
Hyperpigmented, velvety plaques found in intertriginous areas (e.g., neck, axillae). Most commonly associated with what metabolic condition?
a: Insulin resistance (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus) or gastric adenocarcinoma if sudden onset.

q: Painful, erythematous, subcutaneous nodules on the anterior shins. Most common associated condition in a young African American female?
A firm, hyperpigmented nodule on the lower extremity that dimples centrally when pinched (dimple sign). Diagnosis?
Hypertrophic scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, characterized by excessive deposition of Type I and Type III collagen. Diagnosis?
A rapidly growing, friable, red papule that bleeds easily with minor trauma, often appearing during pregnancy or after an injury. Diagnosis?
The most common benign vascular tumor in adults, presenting as small, bright red, dome-shaped papules that increase in number with age. Diagnosis?
A vascular tumor in an infant that grows rapidly during the first few weeks of life and spontaneously regresses by age 5-8 years. Diagnosis?
An HIV patient with a CD4 count <100 cells/mm<sup>3</sup> presents with friable red/purple cutaneous nodules. Biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltrate and bacterial bacilli. Diagnosis and treatment?
An HIV patient presents with violaceous plaques on the skin and hard palate. Biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate and slit-like vascular spaces. Causative agent?
Sudden onset of localized, non-scarring hair loss with "exclamation point" hairs at the periphery of the bald patch. Diagnosis?
What medication used for male pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia) acts as a 5α-reductase inhibitor, preventing conversion of testosterone to DHT?
A patient who frequently uses public pools presents with macerated, scaling, and fissured skin between the toes. Treatment?
a: Topical antifungals (e.g., terbinafine, clotrimazole) for Tinea pedis.

q: A patient taking allopurinol develops fever, facial edema, diffuse morbilliform rash, generalized lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and elevated AST/ALT. Diagnosis?
a: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms).
